 1                     II.    PURPOSE AND SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY
 2   Q.   What is the overall purpose of your direct testimony in this proceeding?

 3   A.   The purpose of my direct testimony is to introduce Xcel Energy’s wildfire

 4        mitigation strategy and support the wildfire mitigation costs included in the Future

 5        Test Year 2. In doing so, I discuss the New Mexico environment and how that relates

 6        to wildfire risk and introduce SPS’s Wildfire Mitigation Plan.

 7   Q.   How does Xcel Energy define risk as it relates to wildfire mitigation?

 8   A.   In the wildfire mitigation context, Xcel Energy defines risk as the magnitude of

 9        potential damage that could result from wildfire in an area under existing conditions

10        (i.e., the susceptibility of the area to potential fire damage). In equation form, this

11        can be presented as:

12                                      risk = likelihood x consequence

13   Q.   Is there an inherent wildfire risk associated with providing electrical service?

14   A.   Yes. Xcel Energy’s operating company utilities generate, transmit, and distribute

15        high voltage electricity across hundreds of thousands of miles of electric

16        transmission and distribution lines. Although the majority of wildfires are caused

17        by factors unrelated to electric utilities, it is a practical reality of providing electric

 1                  III.    NEW MEXICO ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS

 2   Q.      What do you discuss in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.      In this section of my testimony, I discuss the environmental conditions in New

 4           Mexico, and how those conditions result in an elevated level of wildfire risk.

 5   Q.      Are environmental conditions contributing to an increase in wildfire risk

 6           across the United States?

 7   A.      Yes. The United States is in a period of increasing wildfire risk. Beginning in the

 8           2000s, California and the western states started experiencing an increase in

 9           destructive wildfires, as measured by structures burned. According to the United

10           States Global Change Research Program, “climate change, higher temperatures and

11           more severe drought will likely lead to increased area burned in many ecosystems

12           of the western and southeastern United States.” 5 Further, NOAA studies have

13           demonstrated changing weather-induced fuel aridity doubled the burn area of fires

14           after 1984 and has caused a significant lengthening of wildfire seasons. 6

 1           Ultimately, trends in extreme weather events are expected to continue for the

 2           foreseeable future, with associated adverse effects on wildfire risk.

 3   Q.      Does this extend to New Mexico?

 4   A.      Yes. As a whole, New Mexico has experienced some of the greatest increases in the

 5           average number of annual fire weather days since 1973, with some climate

 6           divisions now experiencing approximately two more months of fire weather,

 7           resulting in more than twice the number of fire weather days now compared to 50

 8           years ago. 7 SPS’s service territory is located in the New Mexico Southeastern Plains

 9           climate division as identified by NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental

10           Information. The results of the analysis identified the Southeastern Plains, New

11           Mexico as one of the top ten national locations with the greatest change in fire

12           weather days during the analysis period, with an average increase of 46 days.

13                    The increase in the number of days with heightened wildfire risk has been

14           matched with an increase in wildfire occurrence and severity across the state. The

15           largest wildfire in the state’s history, the Calf Canyon/Hermit’s Peak Fire, occurred

16           in 2022 and burned more than 340,000 acres and over 900 structures. 8 In 2012 the

14        During this phase, grasses are not actively growing, meaning they are not

15        replenishing and maintaining their moisture levels as they do when they are green.

16        Freeze-cured grasses dry out very quickly and are susceptible to ignition from any

 1           spark, which in turn could grow into a wildfire. Grass wildfires can spread very

2            quickly and put residents and communities in the path of danger. 12 Once grass is

3            dry, it has a higher probability of igniting during periods of low relative humidity

 4           and high winds. According to the Western Fire Chiefs Association 13, “peak fire

 5           season” in New Mexico begins in early May and runs through June, until monsoon

 6           season begins. However, according to the New Mexico Forestry Division, the state

 7           is now experiencing fire danger throughout the year due to climate change.” 14

 8           Wind-driven wildfires characterized by the fire behavior described above challenge

 9           even the most robust initial fire suppression attack. High winds also tend to limit

10           the effectiveness of aerial firefighting resources and can cause them to be grounded.

 1   Q.   Does this demonstrate the need to incorporate wildfire mitigation into SPS’s

 2        provision of electric service in New Mexico?

 3   A.   Yes. It is clear that New Mexico’s environment—including that portion served by

 4        SPS—is such that the risk of wildfires is real and likely increasing. A robust wildfire

 5        mitigation strategy therefore is a necessary component of providing safe and

 6        reliable electric service. In the next section of my testimony, I will describe that

 7        strategy, which spans all Xcel Energy operating companies and includes a tailored

 8        approach for the SPS service territory. Strategies are refined to each operating

 9        company territory based on terrain, threats, and other factors unique to the area.

10   Q.   Has SPS developed its own Wildfire Mitigation Plan?

11   A.   Yes. SPS’s current wildfire mitigation plan published in December 2024 (the “2024

12        WMP”) is provided as Attachment PJM-2.

13   Q.   Why did SPS develop the 2024 WMP?

14   A.   SPS is committed to reducing the risk of wildfires to promote the safety and well-

15        being of the customers and communities SPS serves. The 2024 WMP was a natural

16        progression of important SPS objectives: community and employee safety,

17        environmental stewardship, and stakeholder participation. The 2024 WMP built

18        upon existing efforts, integrated industry experience, incorporated new risk

 1           IV.       XCEL ENERGY WILDFIRE MITIGATION STRATEGY

 2   Q.   What do you discuss in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.   In this portion of my Direct Testimony, I discuss how actions to mitigate wildfire

 4        risk are a vital component of SPS’s commitment to providing safe and reliable

5         electric service. In doing so, I will discuss how wildfire presents a challenge to

6         deliver on that obligation and SPS’s overall approach to wildfire risk mitigation. I

7         also discuss certain wildfire mitigation capital costs that are included in the Future

8         Test Year.

 9   Q.   Is wildfire risk reduction a component of providing safe and reliable electric

10        service?

11   A.   Yes. The Xcel Energy operating utilities provide electric service to approximately

12        3.8 million customers across eight states. The environment in those states is

13        changing, with increasing frequency and severity of weather events that affect our

14        operations and ability to serve customers. And as I explained above, New Mexico

15        is not immune from wildfire risk. As a result, SPS is working to improve the safety

16        and resilience of the electric system while also leading the clean energy transition.

17        SPS’s focus on mitigating the threat posed by wildfires directly flows from our

18        commitment to providing safe and reliable electric service to our customers. SPS is

 1        committed to making strategic investments and improvements to support the power

 2        grid and build resilience, but given the threat posed by wildfires, we are placing

 3        heightened focus on mitigating wildfire risk. These efforts include situational

 4        awareness efforts, system resiliency initiatives (i.e., physical mitigation efforts such

 5        as asset inspections and repair/replacement), operational mitigations (i.e., how we

 6        operate the electric system), and communications efforts.

 7   Q.   How does Xcel Energy generally approach wildfire risk mitigation?

 8   A.   Xcel Energy generally employs a layered approach to reducing wildfire risk. Each

 9        layer of defense, or mitigation strategy, provides different benefits that build upon

10        each other, with the overall goal of reducing wildfire risk. This layering of defenses

 3   Q.   Can these activities be placed into categories?

 4   A.   Yes. Wildfire mitigation activities generally fall into one of the following four

 5        categories: (1) situational awareness; (2) system resiliency; (3) operational

 6        mitigations; and (4) customer support. I will discuss each category below.

 7   Q.   Please further describe situational awareness activities.

 8   A.   Situational awareness tools enhance the ability to identify, assess, and respond to

 9        physical or environmental hazards including wildfires. These tools, therefore, are

10        critical to understanding, evaluating, and mitigating wildfire risk. Situational

 1        awareness activities include risk mapping, meteorology and fire science including

 2        proprietary weather station deployment and artificial intelligence (“AI”) cameras.

 3   Q.   Are Xcel Energy’s situational awareness activities organized within one

 4        business area?

 5   A.   Yes. The Xcel Energy Wildfire Risk Organization is responsible for coordination

 6        of overall wildfire-related situational awareness activities.

 7   Q.   What kind of data is collected and reported for wildfire-related situational

 8        awareness?

 9   A.   Xcel Energy collects a variety of data to inform its situational awareness, some of

10        which is focused on pre-ignition conditions and some of which is focused on data

11        after an ignition occurs. Data can include weather and environmental conditions,

12        fire location, fuel moisture, weather warnings (red flag, high wind, fire watch),

13        proximity to Xcel Energy and community assets and condition reports from

14        telephone, email, and in-person communication.

15   Q.   Please describe system resiliency activities.

16   A.   System resiliency activities (also known as system hardening) involve physical

17        mitigation investments to directly reduce the risk of ignitions associated with utility

18        infrastructure. Examples of wildfire-related system resiliency activities include

 1        asset inspections and remediations, line rebuilds, non-expulsion equipment

 2        upgrades, pole replacements, and vegetation management.

 3   Q.   Please describe operational mitigation activities.

 4   A.   Operational mitigations take the electric system as it exists, but through different

 5        system protection settings, reduce the reaction time or fault current created from a

 6        foreign object contact or equipment failure event that could lead to an ignition. The

 7        two primary forms of wildfire operational mitigations are Enhanced Powerline

 8        Safety Settings (“EPSS”) and Public Safety Power Shutoff (“PSPS”).

 9   Q.   Please describe customer support activities.

10   A.   Customer support includes directly informing customers regarding wildfire risk and

11        mitigation activities including PSPS event communications. Customer and

12        Community communications for all-hazard and hazard specific events are detailed

13        in SPS’s Emergency Operations Plan and in confidential Annexes to that plan.

14        Those communications processes entail detailed checklists and standardized

15        communications processes with specific roles clearly identified.

 1   Q.   Is it realistic to expect the elimination of all wildfire risks associated with the

 2        provision of electric service?

 3   A.   No. While wildfire mitigation planning and deployment efforts can reduce the risk

 4        of ignition associated with SPS-owned equipment, some risk will always be

 5        present, particularly because many factors are beyond SPS’s direct control such as

 6        electrical facility contact from foreign objects. Regardless, SPS has a duty to

 7        provide a service in a safe, reliable, and cost-effective manner and reducing wildfire

 8        risk is part of that obligation.

 9   Q.   Do all customers benefit from the wildfire mitigation?

10   A.   Yes. All customers benefit from increased and improved public safety associated

11        with reduced wildfire risk, with customers in higher-risk areas seeing even greater

12        benefits in the form of direct risk reduction. But there are also broader customer

Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS” or the “Company”) is committed to reducing the risk of
wildfires to promote the safety and well-being of the customers and communities we serve. This Wildlife

employee safety, environmental stewardship and stakeholder participation. The Company now

    2. Background
    A. Escalation of Wildfire Risk
The United States is in a period of increasing wildfire risk. Beginning in the 2000s, the United States
started experiencing an increase in destructive wildfires, as measured by structures burned. The
frequency and severity have risen, as characterized by recent wildfires in California, Colorado, Hawaii,
Oregon, Texas and Washington.

According to the Fourth National Climate Assessment produced by the United States Global Change
Research Program, “climate change, higher temperatures and more severe drought will likely lead to
increased area burned in many ecosystems of the western and southeastern United States. By the
mid-21st century, annual area burned is expected to increase 200-300 percent in the contiguous
western United States.”2 Further, NOAA studies have demonstrated that changing weather-induced
fuel aridity doubled the burn area of fires after 1984 and has caused a significant lengthening of wildfire
seasons.3 Ultimately, trends in extreme weather events are expected to continue for the foreseeable
future, with associated adverse effects on wildfire risk. The elevated fire risk of recent years—with large,
destructive fires—shows no sign of subsiding.

    B. Xcel Energy’s Approach to Mitigating Wildfire Risk
As wildfire risk evolves, utility wildfire risk assessment and mitigation is changing, with utilities across
the United States implementing updates to their operational and capital programs in response to global
changing weather patterns, population growth and expanding Wildland Urban Interface (“WUI”). The
changing weather patterns continue to impact vegetation composition and health across the landscape.
Many ecosystems are no longer fire resilient. These changing conditions increase the frequency and
intensity of extreme weather events, and lead to an expansion of higher wildfire risk areas. The WUI
also continues to expand, increasing the probability and exacerbating the costs of wildfire damage to
people and property.

Wildfire risk mitigation remains an evolving process, where improving data analytics and successful
mitigation implementation will enable better wildfire prevention and preparedness. This WMP
represents the continuous refinement, expansion and improvement in SPS’s wildfire mitigation efforts.
The WMP improves upon prior work by integrating practices and experiences of other utilities, new
technologies and new and evolving risk assessment methodologies.

This document details the continued progression and maturity of SPS’s wildfire mitigation program, with
the expanded and complementary mitigation strategies selected to promote risk reduction, in an
expedient and reliable manner. The WMP and its programs and goals are intended to enhance the
safety, reliability and resiliency of the Company’s electric system, respond to a changing climate and
prepare for more frequent and severe weather events. The WMP reflects the Company’s commitment
to public safety through programs that construct, maintain and operate the electric system in a manner
that minimizes the risk of a utility asset being the ignition source for a wildfire.

    D. WRO Risk Evaluation
WRO (wildfirerisk.org) evaluates four risk factors – wildfire likelihood, wildfire intensity, exposure and
susceptibility as depicted and defined below.17

                                                 Figure 12: WRO Risk Factors




Wildfire Likelihood is a probability that any specific location (pixel) may experience wildfire in any
given year. It is based on thousands of fire behavior modeling simulations. In each simulation, factors
contributing to the probability of a fire occurring, including weather, topography and ignitions are varied
based on observations from recent decades.

Wildfire Intensity is a measure of the energy expected from a wildfire. Intensity is largely a condition
of the physical landscape (topography) and vegetative fuel available to burn. For example, a crown fire
on a forested hillside can produce a greater wildfire intensity than grasses on flat ground.

Exposure is the spatial coincidence of wildfire likelihood and intensity with communities. Any
community that is located where wildfire likelihood is greater than zero (i.e., where there is a chance
wildfire could occur) is exposed to wildfire. For example, a home in a flammable forest is exposed to
wildfire risk. Communities can be directly exposed to wildfire from adjacent wildland vegetation, or
indirectly exposed to wildfire from embers and home-to-home ignition.

Susceptibility is the propensity of a home or community to be damaged if a wildfire occurs. WRO uses
a generalized concept of susceptibility for all homes. In other words, WRO assumes all homes that
encounter wildfire will be damaged, and the degree of damage is directly related to wildfire intensity.

   F. Wildfire Risk Tiers
The three Risk Tiers were created to turn the more granular geospatial HFAs into contiguous polygons
useful for a variety of business functions.

Risk Tiers are aggregated from HFAs using broader wildfire risk value ranges to develop a geospatial
wildfire risk visualization variant. A quantile evaluation of the HFA data is used to aggregate the six
HFAs into three tier levels or adjective classes described below.

   1. Tier 1 is the lower risk level tier and includes Fire Resistant and Low HFAs. The Fire
      Resistant tier incorporates areas with significant human development and/or surfaces resistant
      to fire. Examples of fire-resistant areas include bodies of water and waterways (e.g., lakes,
      rivers, etc.) and dense urban areas covered by buildings and surfaces covered in
      asphalt/concrete (e.g., parking lots, surface streets, freeways, etc.). The Lower tier covers areas
      of human development and disturbance that reduce the likelihood of a large, destructive wildfire.
      In general, urban, and semi-urban areas can be classified as Lower as well as barren ground,
      gravel pits, plowed / irrigated fields, feed lots, golf courses, and railroad yards. A catastrophic
      wildfire is still possible in areas designated as “Lower” depending on conditions severity and fire
      suppression resource availability.

   2. Tier 2 is the middle risk level tier, and incorporates Moderate HFAs, where wildfire may
      cause significant damage to human infrastructure due to fuel continuity and/or terrain. The
      resulting wildfire may be less likely to develop substantial momentum depending on severity of
      conditions and fire suppression resources availability.

   3. Tier 3 is the higher risk level tier and contains High HFAs with fuel continuity and population
      density such that a wildfire is likely to rapidly become a large destructive or catastrophic event.

Situational awareness is the ability to monitor weather and environmental conditions to make critical
operational decisions in an effective and timely manner. It covers a broad range of systems and tools
that inform operational and/or response actions for both the transmission and distribution systems.
Currently, Xcel Energy collects a variety of data to inform its situational awareness, some of which is
focused on pre-ignition conditions and some of which is focused on data after an ignition occurs. Data
can include weather conditions, fire location, fuel moisture, weather warnings (red flag, high wind, fire
watch), proximity to Xcel Energy and community assets and condition reports from telephone, email
and in person communication.

In addition to gathering information on current environmental conditions, situational awareness also
extends to understanding which parts of the service territory may be exposed to more consequential
wildfires and when. This information is especially important as SPS expands its EPSS program as part
of its wildfire mitigation activities. EPSS requires more detailed and location-specific assessments of
fire potential, including enhanced meteorological forecasting, along with the gathering of localized
environmental conditions such as wind speed/direction, humidity and fuel moisture.

The following are situational awareness capabilities and tools SPS is using as part of its wildfire
mitigation actions.

Targeted Undergrounding
“Undergrounding” involves reconfiguring all or a portion of an electrical distribution feeder that was built
above ground (or overhead) to an underground construction. Targeted undergrounding mitigates
wildfire risk, and also increases reliability due to less of the feeder being exposed to external elements,
thereby reducing, or avoiding entirely, the causes of many outages (e.g., animal, plant, or vehicle
contacts, or wind, lightning, or icing).

Undergrounding significantly mitigates wildfire risk and improves reliability, but it also is engineering,
design and construction intensive. For example, in some instances, the feeder will need to be
reconfigured from radial taps to a normally open looped system. The Company must identify and obtain
locations for switch cabinets and pad-mount transformers and associated land rights. Undergrounding
also can involve more onerous permitting requirements from various agencies (Bureau of Land
Management, U.S. Forest Service, National Parks Service, state and local governments, etc.).

The targeted undergrounding work in the WMP reflects a balancing of several factors, including SPS’s
experience with undergrounding portions of its distribution system and cost. SPS has experience
undergrounding shorter segments of the distribution system, particularly in flat, less rocky terrain, but
is less experienced in undergrounding large portions of its distribution system (i.e. multiple miles).
These practical considerations, along with others like more substantial permitting and land rights
requirements (as the physical construction footprint is larger due to the need to stage equipment and
disturb more ground) and more complicated logistics (e.g., utility conflicts and geology) all contribute to
SPS developing a targeted approach to undergrounding work.

SPS’s targeted undergrounding proposal also considers cost. Undergrounding, while effectively
mitigating wildfire risk, is relatively expensive due to the intensity of the necessary work. Therefore, the
targeted undergrounding scope of work will be informed by a cost-benefit analysis, with actual
undergrounding being dependent on detailed engineering and study.

Distribution Non-Expulsion Upgrades
When a distribution feeder experiences a fault and an overcurrent occurs, fuses on the feeder are
designed to open and isolate the fault, limiting further damage to other equipment. An expulsion fuse
is designed to quench the arc, with material being expelled out of the fuse tube. The material being
expelled can be hot and therefore presents an ignition risk when expelled in proximity to dry or cured
vegetation.

Lightning arresters are devices installed to ground lightning surges. They direct the excess energy from
a lightning strike to ground, protecting pole top equipment such as transformers. Arresters can fail when
lightning surge energy exceeds their capacity, or due to repeated operations. When an arrester fails at

    i. Enhanced Powerline Safety Settings Program
EPSS is the most sophisticated form of Wildfire Safety Operations (WSO). All forms of WSO provide
for disabling automatic reclosing on relays and reclosers that are normally set to automatically reclose.
More sophisticated versions of WSO enable faster (but not necessarily coordinating) trip settings for
relays and reclosers that have those capabilities.

EPSS modifies settings in the relays and reclosers on the distribution system (both within the substation
and outside the substation on the feeder) to create a wildfire-specific operating mode. When EPSS is
activated, relays and reclosers are more sensitive to electrical faults and react faster to those faults
(compared to normal settings in each such device). EPSS, when activated, also disables reclosing in
relays and reclosers that would normally be set to automatically reclose after tripping because of a
fault. Ultimately, EPSS allows for power lines to remain in-service during periods of elevated wildfire
risks, but with protection settings that mitigate the wildfire risk.

tree limb falling on a power line) under normal circumstances. Under normal settings, the electrical fault
causes the fuse to trip, de-energizing the line downstream. With the fuse tripping, the recloser and
substation relay generally will not trip, as they are set to clear faults slower than the downstream fuses.
Also, if the recloser and substation relay trip (generally for a fault upstream of any fuses), they will
automatically reclose one or more times.

EPSS and WSO implement protection settings that could de-energize more of the Company’s system
following an electrical fault. EPSS and WSO therefore are only activated during conditions of elevated
wildfire risk. That activation can occur either by automation or manually.47F21

Distribution lines must be physically inspected if a fault is detected, and a sectionalizing protective
device operates during a WSO event (including EPSS events). When a recloser or breaker trips while
EPSS is active, the distribution operations team will patrol and restore the outage, including initiating
corrective maintenance if needed, and will document any visible cause of the trip in writing and with
imagery. If there is a second trip on the same line segment within five minutes of the line being
reenergized (including a trip immediately upon the line being reenergized), a review will be conducted
with the distribution control center and distribution operations leadership to determine the next steps
for restoration. Patrols and restorations after daylight hours will be at the discretion of the distribution
control center and distribution operations leadership based on factors such as weather conditions,
terrain and geography of the service territory, lighting and other operational factors limiting the ability
to fully assess the line. The Company has developed and implemented a process to capture the causes
of outages that occur while EPSS is activated for assessment and quantification of the effectiveness of
EPSS.

The Company plans to enhance and expand its communication and engagement with its customers,

The Company has started and will continue to conduct informational sessions and present its WMP to

The Company continues to build its outreach, education, and engagement efforts. Stakeholder
